body: Why is the year of Muhammad's birth (**570/71 CE**) referred to as the **'Year of the Elephant'**?
answer:
> [!answer]
> Because in that year **Abraha**, the Abyssinian (Christian) ruler of **Yemen**, marched on **Mecca** with an army including **war elephants** to **destroy the Ka'bah**. The attack failed: tradition says Allah sent **flocks of birds pelting stones** (Qur'an **Surah al-Fil**, 'The Elephant'), and the army was destroyed. Muhammad was born that year.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The event enhanced Mecca's and the Quraysh's prestige as protectors of the Ka'bah. Muslims see it as a sign of divine protection of the sanctuary before the Prophet's birth.

## Simplified explanation

That year an army with **elephants** tried to destroy the **Ka'bah** in Mecca and failed, and Muhammad was born.

body: Mention **two benefits** the ancient **Sudanese empires** (Ghana, Mali, Songhai) derived from Islam.
answer:
> [!answer]
> Any two: **literacy in Arabic**, enabling **record-keeping and administration** · expanded **trans-Saharan trade** and contacts with North Africa and the Middle East · **centres of learning** (Timbuktu, Djenne, Sankore) · a **legal system** (Shari'a) and trained judges (qadis) · **diplomatic relations** and prestige (e.g. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage, 1324) · a unifying **ideology** for diverse peoples.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Rulers often adopted Islam (fully or partly) because Muslim scribes, traders and scholars brought **administrative, commercial and diplomatic advantages**, while many subjects kept traditional religion: a pattern of court Islam.

## Simplified explanation

Islam brought **reading and writing**, **more trade**, **great schools** like Timbuktu, and **laws**.

body: Mention the **two theories** on the **introduction of Islam to Ghana**, and the **two ethnic groups** to whom you would attribute its promotion.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Theories:** (1) Islam came from the **north-west** through **Mande (Wangara/Dyula) traders and clerics** from the Mali empire, along the **gold and kola trade routes** (to Begho, Bono, Gonja), about the 14th–15th centuries. (2) Islam came from the **north-east** through **Hausa** traders and clerics from **Hausaland/Borno**, especially from the 17th–18th centuries.
>
> **Ethnic groups:** the **Wangara/Dyula (Mande)** and the **Hausa**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Islam spread mainly by **peaceful trade and clerical service** to chiefs (prayers, amulets, literacy), not conquest. Mande influence shaped Gonja and Dagbon Islam; Hausa influence later dominated the **zongo** communities of southern towns (Kumasi, Accra).

## Simplified explanation

Islam came to Ghana with **traders**: the **Wangara (Mande)** from the north-west and the **Hausa** from the north-east.

body: Name the **three main classes** of people that appeared in **Gonja** society as a result of Islamic influences.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. The **ruling class (Ngbanya)**: the chiefly estate. 2. The **Muslim class (Karamo/Mallams)**: clerics and scholars. 3. The **commoners (Nyemase)**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Gonja was founded (c. 16th century) by Mande warriors (Ndewura Jakpa) accompanied by **Muslim clerics**, who became a distinct estate serving the court with prayers, advice and literacy alongside rulers and commoners.

## Simplified explanation

Gonja had **rulers**, **Muslim scholars** and **ordinary people**.

body: Explain the term **Karamo**. Who were the **Sharifs (Shurafa')**?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Karamo** (Mande term) is a **Muslim cleric/scholar**: a learned man who teaches the Qur'an, leads prayers, advises chiefs, and prepares **charms/amulets** and prayers for clients.
>
> **Sharifs (Shurafa')** are **descendants of the Prophet Muhammad** (through his daughter **Fatima** and **Ali**), held in high respect in Muslim societies.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Karamos were key agents of Islamisation in Ghana through **service to rulers**. Sharifian lineages (some claimed in northern Ghana) carried religious prestige (_baraka_).

## Simplified explanation

A **Karamo** is a Muslim **teacher/cleric**. The **Sharifs** are **descendants of Prophet Muhammad**.

body: Mention **two factors** that have facilitated the **growth of Islam** in modern Ghana, and state the names of any **two second-cycle institutions** established by Muslims.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Factors:** **trade and migration** (zongos in southern towns) · **Islamic education** (Arabic and English–Arabic schools) · **intermarriage** · **religious freedom** under the Constitution · **da'wah** and media · support from Muslim organisations and countries (scholarships, mosques) · Ahmadiyya schools and hospitals.
>
> **Institutions:** **T. I. Ahmadiyya Senior High School** (Kumasi) · **Islamic Senior High School** (Kumasi) · other Ahmadiyya and Islamic SHSs.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Muslims are about **20% of Ghana's population** (2021 census). Modern growth is linked to **formal education** (Islamic Education Unit of the GES), urban zongos and reform movements (Ahmadiyya, Ahlus-Sunnah).

## Simplified explanation

Islam grows through **trade, Islamic schools, marriage and religious freedom**. Examples of Muslim schools: **T.I. Ahmadiyya SHS** and **Islamic SHS**, Kumasi.

body: Identify **two contributions** of Muslims to **national politics** in Ghana.
answer:
> [!answer]
> Any two: formation of the **Muslim Association Party (1954)**, which merged into the **United Party** opposition · Muslims serving in **high office** (e.g. Vice-Presidents **Alhaji Aliu Mahama** and **Dr Mahamudu Bawumia**, ministers, MPs) · promotion of **peace and national unity** (the National Chief Imam's role in elections and interfaith peace) · participation in governance at local level · the **Eid** festivals made **national holidays**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Muslim political participation evolved from a communal party (MAP) to integration in national parties, with the **National Chief Imam** (Sheikh Osmanu Nuhu Sharubutu) recognised as a symbol of interfaith peace.

## Simplified explanation

Muslims formed the **Muslim Association Party**, have served as **Vice-Presidents and ministers**, and work for **peace**.

body: Evaluate **three factors** that have contributed to the **growth of Islam in Ghana**.
answer:
1. **Trade:** Muslim traders (Wangara/Dyula, Hausa) along the **gold, kola and salt routes** settled in market towns, built mosques and attracted converts; **zongos** spread Islam to southern Ghana.
2. **Service of clerics to chiefs:** Muslim scholars offered **prayers, amulets, literacy and advice** to rulers (Gonja, Dagbon, Asante), winning **royal patronage** and prestige.
3. **Islamic education:** Qur'anic schools (makaranta), **English–Arabic schools**, and Islamic SHSs and universities train generations.
4. **Intermarriage and family:** marriage with local people and large families increase the Muslim population.
5. **Migration and urbanisation:** northern and Sahelian migrants to southern cities.
6. **Religious freedom and peaceful coexistence** under Ghana's constitutions.
7. **Reform movements and external support:** the Ahmadiyya, Ahlus-Sunnah wal-Jama'a, NGOs and Middle Eastern funding for mosques, schools and scholarships; media da'wah.

> [!answer]
> Trade and zongos, clerics' service to chiefs, Islamic education, intermarriage, migration and urbanisation, religious freedom, and reform movements and external support.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Ghanaian Islam spread largely **peacefully**, by trade, clerical service and accommodation, unlike the jihadist expansions elsewhere in West Africa. 'Evaluate' requires judging relative importance: **trade** explains the initial spread; **education and organisation** explain modern growth.

## Simplified explanation

Islam grew because **traders** brought it, **chiefs** valued Muslim scholars, **Islamic schools** taught it, and people **married and moved**, with freedom to worship.

body: Assess **three contributions** of the **Ahmadiyya Movement** to the development of Ghanaian society.
answer:
1. **Education:** pioneered **modern (Western-style) secular education** for Muslims: many basic schools and SHSs, e.g. **T. I. Ahmadiyya SHS (Kumasi)**, and a university college, combining Islamic and secular subjects.
2. **Health care:** hospitals and clinics (e.g. **Ahmadiyya Muslim hospitals** at Agona Swedru, Techiman, Asokore, Daboase), serving all Ghanaians regardless of religion.
3. **Religious literature and translation:** translated the **Qur'an into Ghanaian languages** (e.g. Twi) and English, and published Islamic literature, promoting understanding.
4. **Interfaith dialogue and peace:** promotes tolerance ('Love for all, hatred for none').
5. **Social services:** humanitarian relief, water projects, agriculture, blood donation.

> [!answer]
> Modern schools (e.g. T.I. Ahmadiyya SHS), hospitals and clinics, translations of the Qur'an into local languages and English, interfaith peace, and social and humanitarian services.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The Ahmadiyya mission (arrived in the Gold Coast **1921**, from India) brought a reformist model: **education in English**, organisation and mass literature. It gained a following among the Fante. Mainstream Muslims reject some Ahmadi doctrines (on prophethood), but its social contributions are widely acknowledged.

## Simplified explanation

The Ahmadiyya built **schools and hospitals**, **translated the Qur'an** into local languages, and preaches **peace**.

body: List the **five major practices** (pillars) of Muslims in Ghana and explain any **three** in detail.
answer:
**The Five Pillars of Islam:**
1. **Shahada:** the **declaration of faith**: 'There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.' Reciting it sincerely makes one a Muslim; it is repeated in daily prayers and whispered to newborns.
2. **Salat:** the **five daily prayers** (Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha) facing **Mecca (qibla)**, after **ablution (wudu)**; Friday congregational prayer (Jumu'ah) at the mosque. It builds discipline and constant remembrance of God.
3. **Zakat:** **obligatory almsgiving**, about **2.5%** of qualifying wealth annually, given to the poor and needy; it purifies wealth and promotes social justice.
4. **Sawm:** **fasting in the month of Ramadan**, from dawn to sunset (no food, drink or sex), ending with **Eid al-Fitr**; it teaches self-control, empathy for the poor and piety.
5. **Hajj:** the **pilgrimage to Mecca** once in a lifetime for those **physically and financially able**, in Dhul-Hijjah, ending with **Eid al-Adha**; it symbolises unity and equality of Muslims.

> [!answer]
> Shahada (faith), Salat (five daily prayers), Zakat (almsgiving), Sawm (Ramadan fast), Hajj (pilgrimage); explain three with their meaning, practice and significance.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In Ghana the pillars are visible in public life: Friday prayers, Ramadan and **Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha as national holidays**, Hajj flights organised by the Hajj Board, and zakat committees. Ghanaian Muslims also observe Maulid (the Prophet's birthday) and life-cycle rites (naming, marriage, funerals).

## Simplified explanation

Muslims **declare their faith**, **pray five times a day**, **give to the poor**, **fast in Ramadan**, and **go on pilgrimage to Mecca** if they can.

body: Examine **three contributions** Islam has made to the **socio-cultural life** of contemporary Ghanaian society.
answer:
1. **Festivals and public holidays:** **Eid al-Fitr** and **Eid al-Adha** are national holidays; communal prayers and feasting promote unity.
2. **Dress and fashion:** the **smock-like jalabiya**, kaftans, turbans, hijab and the popularity of northern and Hausa styles.
3. **Names and language:** Islamic/Arabic names (Ibrahim, Fatima, Mohammed), and **loanwords** in Ghanaian languages (Hausa as the lingua franca of zongos).
4. **Education and literacy:** Qur'anic and English–Arabic schools; Arabic scholarship.
5. **Moral and social values:** emphasis on modesty, abstinence from alcohol, charity (zakat, sadaqa), hospitality and respect for elders.
6. **Architecture:** Sudanese-style mosques (e.g. **Larabanga Mosque**, Wa, Bole), now tourist attractions.
7. **Commerce and food culture:** trading networks, kola trade; foods such as **waakye, tuo zaafi, kebabs (chichinga), koko**, and halal practice.
8. **Peaceful coexistence:** interfaith marriage and cooperation; the National Chief Imam's peace role.

> [!answer]
> Eid holidays, dress and fashion, Arabic names and loanwords, Islamic education, moral values, Sudanese-style architecture, trade and food culture, and interfaith peace.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Islam's cultural influence in Ghana is long-standing in the **north** (Dagbon, Gonja, Wa, where Islamic and traditional practices intertwine in festivals like Damba) and increasingly visible in **southern cities** through zongos, Hausa culture and media.

## Simplified explanation

Islam gave Ghana **Eid holidays**, **clothes**, **names**, **foods**, **old mosques** like Larabanga, and **values** like charity and modesty.
